parts.title: Passage — The Lost Photographs

segments.say: Lesson two. The lost photographs. Listening practice.
You will hear a story about a student and her photographs. The story happened in the past. You will hear it two times. Do not read the text. Listen only.

Last year, Maha was a student at a college in Gaza. She studied design, and she loved her work. Every week she took photographs of her city - the market, the sea, the old streets. She kept all of them on her phone.

One morning in May, Maha put her phone in her bag and went to college. At eleven o'clock, she opened the bag. The phone was not there. She looked everywhere, but she did not find it.

She was sad about the phone, but she was much sadder about the photographs. There were more than two thousand of them, and she had no other copy. Three years of work disappeared in one morning.

Her teacher listened to her story and asked one question: "Did you have a backup?" Maha did not know the word. The teacher explained it in a simple way. A backup is a second copy of your files in another place. If you lose the first copy, you still have the second one.

That week, Maha learned how to make backups. She copied her new photographs to a laptop. She also copied the most important ones to a memory card, and she kept the card at home. When the internet was good, she sent some folders to an online drive.

Maha still remembers her lost photographs. But now she says the same thing to every new student: "Your phone is not a safe place. It is only one place."

Last year, Maha was a student at a college in Gaza. She studied design, and she loved her work. Every week she took photographs of her city — the market, the sea, the old streets. She kept all of them on her phone.

**[B]** She was sad about the phone, but she was much sadder about the photographs. There were more than two thousand of them, and she had no other copy. Three years of work disappeared in one morning.

**[C]** Her teacher listened to her story and asked one question: "Did you have a backup?" Maha did not know the word. The teacher explained it in a simple way. A backup is a second copy of your files in another place. If you lose the first copy, you still have the second one.

parts.title: Grammar — the past simple
parts.markdown:
We use the past simple for a finished action in the past: *Last year she **studied** design.*

### 3.1 Regular verbs — add **-ed**

| Now | Last year |
|---|---|
| study | studi**ed** |
| love | lov**ed** |
| look | look**ed** |
| copy | copi**ed** |
| explain | explain**ed** |
| disappear | disappear**ed** |
| learn | learn**ed** |
| remember | remember**ed** |

### 3.2 Irregular verbs — you must learn each one

| Now | Last year |
|---|---|
| is / are | **was / were** |
| take | **took** |
| keep | **kept** |
| put | **put** |
| go | **went** |
| open | opened *(regular)* |
| find | **found** |
| have | **had** |
| say | **said** |
| send | **sent** |

### 3.4 Negative and question

| | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Negative | **did not** + base verb | She **did not find** it. (not *did not found*) |
| Question | **Did** + person + base verb | **Did** you **have** a backup? |

### Teacher Notes {: #teacher-notes }

**What changed from Lesson 1.** The passage grew from 185 to 244 words, the tense moved from present simple to past simple, and a seventh question type (sentence insertion) joined the set. Everything else — the order of the sessions, the five original TOEFL question types, the self-report — is deliberately identical, so only one thing is new at a time.

**The one real difficulty.** Not the vocabulary: the *did not + base verb* rule. Arabic speakers very often produce *did not found*, because the past is already marked once. Correct it every time this week, even in speech, and it usually settles by Lesson 4.

**Why this story.** The student is a postgraduate applying for an exchange: within a year they will be carrying their own application files, scans and transcripts between machines. The passage teaches the vocabulary of that problem while teaching the tense.

**Success criteria for Lesson 2.** The student should be able to:

- answer L1–L4 correctly on the second hearing;
- retell the story in 4–5 past-simple sentences without the text;
- form a correct negative and a correct question in the past simple;
- use 10 of the 14 key words in their own sentence;
- write 8 sentences about a personal past event with fewer than 4 tense errors.

**If it is too easy:** Lesson 3 goes to 320 words with past continuous (*while she was walking*), and the MCQ set adds a "purpose of the paragraph" question.
**If it is too hard:** keep the same passage for a second week, drop the sentence-insertion question, and drill only Session 3.1 and 3.4.

**A note on Lesson 1 words.** The self-report asks which Lesson 1 words have been forgotten on purpose, and `05-ed-sounds.mp3`'s companion — the last minute of `03-vocabulary.mp3` — brings five Lesson 1 words back with a five-second gap before the meaning is given. Keep that habit every week: spaced recall, not repetition inside one week, is what moves vocabulary into long-term memory.
